Where, why and how

  • Where: between the cold-working stages of low-carbon steel thin products: cold-rolled sheet and strip (galvanised, tinplate and colour-coated sheet), cold-drawn wire and tube, multi-stage deep drawing.
  • Why: cold rolling multiplies dislocations, so strength and hardness rise and ductility falls almost to zero (book Fig 2.10: about 750 MPa at only a few per cent strain, against about 350 MPa and 25% strain after annealing). Further rolling would crack the edges, break the strip and need huge roll forces. Process annealing restores ductility so working can continue. It is cheaper than full annealing or normalising: no austenitising and no furnace cooling.
  • How: heat below \mathrm{A_1} (727^\circ\mathrm{C}) but above the recrystallisation temperature, about 550 to 650^\circ\mathrm{C} for heavily cold-rolled low-C steel; hold briefly; cool. Coils are batch annealed in bell furnaces or run through continuous annealing lines in a non-oxidising \mathrm{H_2}-\mathrm{N_2} atmosphere, because thin strip must not oxidise. A fine grain is the target.

The 3 mm to 75 µm route

Total reduction = (3 - 0.075)/3 = 97.5\% (true strain \ln 40 = 3.7). Low-C strip takes only about 70 to 80% per stage, so for example: 3.0 to 0.60 mm (80%), anneal, 0.60 to 0.15 mm (75%), anneal, 0.15 to 0.075 mm (50%), final anneal in the continuous galvanising and colour-coating line. Every anneal costs energy, furnace time, protective gas and handling, so each must restore full ductility in one pass.

Fully cold-rolled structure: ferrite (about 90%) flattened into pancake grains along the rolling direction with deformation bands; the roughly 10% pearlite elongated, its lamellae bent and broken. Below the first dashed line only recovery occurs: dislocations rearrange into sub-grains and some stress is relieved, but grains and hardness barely change.

Point (1): inside the recrystallisation range

  • Old and new grain curves cross: about half the structure is small new strain-free grains, nucleated at deformation bands and old boundaries; the rest is still elongated, work-hardened grains.
  • Strength and hardness only partly reduced, ductility partly restored, mixed grain size.
  • Cheapest anneal and no oxidation, but the strip cannot take the next large reduction: edge cracks, strip breaks, uneven thinning and poor flatness, so more passes and more anneals. Overall cost rises and properties vary along the coil.

Point (2): just after recrystallisation is complete

  • 100% fine, equiaxed, strain-free ferrite with only slight growth; cementite of the deformed pearlite partly spheroidised (prior cold work speeds this).
  • Hardness and strength at the annealed level, ductility fully restored, fine grain keeps good strength and toughness.
  • Moderate temperature and time, little oxidation, maximum next reduction, so the fewest anneals; smooth surface for coating. The optimum.

Point (3): deep in the grain-growth range

  • Coarse equiaxed ferrite; carbides coarsen at the boundaries.
  • Lowest strength. Coarse grains give orange-peel roughening on further rolling and forming, poor paint appearance and adhesion, and at 75 µm only a few grains across the thickness: anisotropy, tearing and pinholes.
  • Highest energy, longest cycle, more scale (pickling and yield loss) and coil-wrap sticking in batch annealing. Highest cost and worst quality.

Conclusion: process anneal at point (2) between passes; finish at (2) for formable sheet, or use only a recovery anneal if a full-hard grade is wanted.

2.html:
Assumptions (no composition is printed): plain carbon steel with 1.2% C and 0.4% Mn, hardened from 770^\circ\mathrm{C} (about \mathrm{Ac_1} + 40^\circ\mathrm{C}) by water quenching to 25^\circ\mathrm{C}.

Reasons for the triple-phase structure

  1. The stock is hypereutectoid. Figure 2 shows dark pearlite colonies outlined by a white, continuous network of proeutectoid cementite on the prior austenite grain boundaries.
  2. Undissolved cementite. A hypereutectoid steel is hardened from the \gamma + \mathrm{Fe_3C} field, not above Acm. At 770^\circ\mathrm{C} the pearlite becomes austenite but the network and coarse carbides cannot all dissolve, so cementite survives the quench (white particles in Figure 3). A short soak leaves even more.
  3. Martensite. The austenite was cooled faster than the critical rate (no pearlite or bainite in Figure 3), so it sheared to BCT martensite.
  4. Retained austenite (RA). At 770^\circ\mathrm{C} the austenite is saturated at about 0.9% C (Acm line), so M_s \approx 520 - 320(0.9) - 50(0.4) = 212^\circ\mathrm{C} and M_f is below room temperature. Transformation stops at 25^\circ\mathrm{C} with about 10 to 15% austenite left. A delay or slow cooling between M_s and M_f stabilises it further.

Schedule for a dual-phase (martensite + cementite) structure

  1. Break the network: normalise from about 900^\circ\mathrm{C} (above Acm, about 860^\circ\mathrm{C}), air cool; then spheroidise (cycle about \mathrm{A_1}, 700 to 750^\circ\mathrm{C}, furnace cool).
  2. Harden: austenitise at 770^\circ\mathrm{C}, soak about 1 h per 25 mm, quench in brine or water.
  3. Sub-zero treat at once: -80^\circ\mathrm{C} (dry ice) or -196^\circ\mathrm{C} (liquid nitrogen), below M_f, to turn the RA into martensite.
  4. Temper at 150 to 200^\circ\mathrm{C} for 1 to 2 h.

Result: tempered martensite + spheroidal cementite, about 62 to 64 HRC, no RA, good wear resistance and dimensional stability. Martensite + RA could be made by austenitising above Acm to dissolve all cementite, but that gives coarse plate martensite, more RA and quench cracks, so it is not advised.

Residual stress

Given: Table 1 atomic volumes; E = 210\ \mathrm{GPa}; RA 12% (the book's value for about 0.9% C).

Find: volume change on hardening and the stress it can lock in.

Step 1. Phase amounts (lever rule; weight fractions used as Fe-atom fractions):

\begin{aligned} \text{stock: } W_{\mathrm{P}} &= \frac{6.67 - 1.2}{6.67 - 0.76} = 0.926, \quad W_{\mathrm{Fe_3C}} = 0.074 \\ \text{quenched: } W_{\mathrm{Fe_3C}} &= \frac{1.2 - 0.9}{6.67 - 0.9} = 0.052, \quad W_{\gamma} = 0.12, \quad W_{\mathrm{M}} = 1 - 0.052 - 0.12 = 0.828 \end{aligned}

Step 2. Mean atomic volume (\mathring{\mathrm{A}}^{3} per Fe atom):

\begin{aligned} V_0 &= 0.926(11.916) + 0.074(12.769) = 11.980 \\ V_{\mathrm{M}} &= 11.789 + 0.370(0.9) = 12.122, \quad V_{\gamma} = 11.401 + 0.329(0.9) = 11.697 \\ V_1 &= 0.052(12.769) + 0.828(12.122) + 0.12(11.697) = 12.105 \end{aligned}

Step 3. Volume change:

\frac{\Delta V}{V} = \frac{12.105 - 11.980}{11.980} = 0.0104 = 1.04\%

The slide formula, written with fractions, agrees: 0.828(1.68)(0.9) + 0.12(-4.64 + 2.21 \times 0.9) = 0.93\%.

Step 4. Stress: the linear strain is one third of the volume strain.

\begin{aligned} \varepsilon &= \tfrac{1}{3}\,\frac{\Delta V}{V} = 3.48\times10^{-3} \\ \sigma &= E\varepsilon = (210\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{MPa})(3.48\times10^{-3}) = 731\ \mathrm{MPa} \end{aligned}

Answer: \Delta V/V \approx +1.0\% and a retained stress of about 0.7\ \mathrm{GPa} (650 to 730 MPa), enough to distort or crack the part, so it must be tempered without delay.

2.watch:
• The carbon content is not printed. Any hypereutectoid value (1.0 to 1.4% C) is fine if stated; the method and the order of the answer (about 1% volume growth, several hundred MPa) stay the same.
  • The 12% RA is read from the book's RA-against-carbon graph for 0.9% C; the Koistinen-Marburger estimate e^{-0.011(212 - 25)} = 0.13 agrees.
  • The stress is an upper bound: it assumes the whole transformation strain is held elastically. Plastic flow of the softer phases and the different timing of surface and core transformation lower the real value.
  • A classical ferrite + martensite dual-phase structure needs a hypoeutectoid steel annealed between Ac1 and Ac3; it cannot be made from this steel.

Alloying has moved gear A's noses far to the right and pushed M_s and M_f down; gear B has very low hardenability.

Reading Figure 5 (gears of the probe size)

  • #2 oil: reaches 620^\circ\mathrm{C} in about 8.5 s at 80 to 100^\circ\mathrm{C} (9.8 s at 20^\circ\mathrm{C}) and 390^\circ\mathrm{C} in about 15 s. A hot bath has lower viscosity and breaks the vapour blanket sooner, so it is fastest through the nose region.
  • Water: reaches 540^\circ\mathrm{C} in about 2.7 s at 20^\circ\mathrm{C}, 3.8 s at 40^\circ\mathrm{C}, 6 s at 60^\circ\mathrm{C}; at 80 to 99.5^\circ\mathrm{C} a stable vapour blanket holds the part near 650 to 700^\circ\mathrm{C}, so 540^\circ\mathrm{C} is reached only after about 16 s and 36 s.

Gear A schedule

  1. Preheat at 600 to 650^\circ\mathrm{C} (high C and alloy, CE above 0.7).
  2. Austenitise at about 830^\circ\mathrm{C} (about 60 K above the C-curve limit near 770^\circ\mathrm{C}), soak 60 + D min, protective atmosphere.
  3. Quench in agitated #2 oil at about 80^\circ\mathrm{C} (60 to 100^\circ\mathrm{C}). Below about 770^\circ\mathrm{C} it needs only about 5 s to pass 620^\circ\mathrm{C} (nose 13 s) and 12 s to pass 390^\circ\mathrm{C} (bainite nose 60 s): no pearlite or bainite. The bath sits just below M_s, so surface and core transform almost together: least distortion. Water is unnecessary and would crack the gear.
  4. At 20^\circ\mathrm{C} the steel is only 80^\circ\mathrm{C} below M_s: f_M = 1 - e^{-0.011(100 - 20)} \approx 0.59, so about 40% austenite is retained. Cold treat at once at -70 to -100^\circ\mathrm{C} (below M_f), 1 h per 3 cm.
  5. Temper immediately at 150 to 200^\circ\mathrm{C}, twice.

Gear B schedule

  1. Austenitise at 800 to 820^\circ\mathrm{C} (A_3 + 30 to 50), soak 60 + D min.
  2. Quench in violently agitated water at about 20^\circ\mathrm{C} (keep below 30^\circ\mathrm{C}; 10% brine is better). The nose needs
\frac{727 - 540}{0.75} \approx 250^\circ\mathrm{C\,s^{-1}};

water at 20^\circ\mathrm{C} gives about (727 - 540)/1.55 \approx 120^\circ\mathrm{C\,s^{-1}} at the probe position, oil about a tenth of that. The high M_s means martensite forms while the part is still hot and plastic, so this medium-carbon gear tolerates the severe quench better than gear A would. Only the coldest water fully hardens the teeth and surface; hot water (\geq 60^\circ\mathrm{C}) or oil gives ferrite and pearlite.

  1. M_f \approx 245^\circ\mathrm{C} is above room temperature: no sub-zero treatment. Temper at once (about 200^\circ\mathrm{C} for wear, higher for tougher teeth).

As-quenched microstructures

  • Gear A: fine plate (needle) martensite with about 40% white retained austenite between the plates, plus any undissolved carbides; after cold treatment, nearly all martensite.
  • Gear B: lath martensite in packets at the teeth and surface; deeper, martensite with some upper bainite, fine pearlite and grain-boundary ferrite, giving a U-shaped hardness profile.

Mn is present in every steel (up to 1.65% in carbon steels), so its level must be matched to the product.

Dual behaviour of Mn

BeneficialHarmful
Deoxidiser and desulphuriser: high-melting MnS instead of FeS, no hot shortness when Mn/S is at least 8 (10 for welding)Above about 2%: quench cracking from high hardenability and transformation stresses
Solid-solution strengthening; refines ferrite and pearlite by lowering the \gamma \to \alpha temperaturePromotes temper embrittlement: drives P, Sn, Sb, As to prior-austenite boundaries at 375 to 575^\circ\mathrm{C}
Lowers the DBTT: about 120^\circ\mathrm{C} at 0% Mn to about -30^\circ\mathrm{C} at 2% Mn (slide 46)Raises the carbon equivalent \mathrm{CE} = \mathrm{C} + \mathrm{Mn}/6 + \dots: hard HAZ, cold cracking; below 0.30% Mn, weld porosity and hot cracks
Strong hardenability agent (factor 1 + 3.33\,\%\mathrm{Mn}): oil instead of water quenchingLowers Ms: retained austenite in high-C, high-Mn steels
Austenite stabiliser: at 11 to 14% Mn, tough austenite that work hardensMnS stringers (anisotropy), segregation and banding

Product 1: welded structural steel (plates, sections and rebar for bridges and buildings). Needs strength, toughness and weldability.

  • Customised Mn: 0.30 to 0.80% for ordinary 0.20 to 0.25% C steel; up to about 1.5% only when C is 0.18% or less (Nb or V HSLA), so that CE stays at or below about 0.43 (0.5 is the limit for defect-free welding); Mn/S at least 10.
  • Benefit used: strength, fine grain, low DBTT. Harm avoided: HAZ martensite and cold cracking, porosity and hot cracks in the weld bead.

Product 2: quenched and tempered shafts, axles, gears and oil-hardening tools (4140, 1340, O1). Need through-hardening and toughness after tempering.

  • Customised Mn: 0.75 to 1.0% with Cr-Mo (4140), at most about 1.9% in Mn steels (1340), 1.0 to 1.4% in O1; never above about 2%.
  • Benefit used: hardenability, so an oil quench hardens the core with little distortion. Harm avoided: P below about 0.02% and very low Sn, Sb, As, plus 0.15 to 0.3% Mo, against temper embrittlement; temper above the embrittling range and cool fast through 375 to 575^\circ\mathrm{C}; sub-zero treatment for high-C grades to remove retained austenite.

Product 3: impact-wear parts (railway crossings, crusher jaws, excavator teeth: Hadfield steel). Need a hard wearing surface on a tough body.

  • Customised Mn: 11 to 14% with 1.0 to 1.4% C (Mn/C about 10). Water toughening (1000 to 1100^\circ\mathrm{C}, water quench) dissolves the carbides and gives soft (about 200 HB), tough austenite; impact in service work hardens the surface to about 500 HB.
  • Harm avoided: Mn below about 10% would allow brittle martensite; P, Sn and Sb kept very low because they segregate and crack crossings; no reheating above about 300^\circ\mathrm{C} in welding or service, which would precipitate grain-boundary carbides. Parts are cast to shape and ground.

Principle: the service need sets the Mn level (moderate for welding, medium for hardening, high for impact wear), and its harmful side is held off by limits on C, S and P and by the heat treatment.

5a.html:
Starting point. Figure 6 ranks surface hardness only: carburised steel about 700 to 800 HV, against about 1500 to 2300 HV for boronised steel, about 2000 HV for TiN and over 3000 HV for TiCN and TD coatings. Hardness is one requirement among several, so the case was built as follows.

1. Technological responsibilities

  • What the part needs. Simple ball-bearing parts need 58 to 64 HRC (about 650 to 800 HV), a case deep enough for the Hertzian shear stress that peaks below the surface, a tough core and compressive surface stress for rolling-contact fatigue. Carburising and hardening already give this.
  • Thin hard layers fail here. Coatings (TiN, CrN, TiCN, TD) are a few micrometres thick; under rolling contact the softer substrate yields below them and they crack and spall (eggshell effect), and they cannot be finish-ground.
  • Brittle layers. Boride layers (FeB in tension, slide 31) are brittle and spall under cyclic contact; their thickness is hard to control.
  • Material mismatch. The plant casts and rolls plain carbon steel. Nitriding needs Al, Cr or Mo steels ("nitrided alloy steel"), and TD and PVD need tool-steel substrates; switching would change the upstream grades.
  • Process risk. New, untried processes bring new defects and quality-control needs.

2. Economic condition

  • Pack carburising needs only boxes, an ordinary furnace and cheap charcoal, coke and \mathrm{BaCO_3}, run by trained staff.
  • PVD, CVD, TD or boronising need vacuum or special reactors, imported consumables and spares, retraining and downtime: high capital, slow return.
  • Simple bearing parts are low-value; customers will not pay for hardness they did not ask for, and brittle failures would bring warranty costs.

3. Relevance

  • The chart's top techniques are for cutting tools, dies and severe abrasion, not for rolling contact.
  • Pack carburising fits the plant's steel, volume and skills, and can be upgraded step by step (controlled compound, direct quench, later gas carburising).

Conclusion: keep pack carburising; it gives the right, not the highest, hardness at the lowest cost.

5b.html:
Why carburised parts must be hardened

Carburising (900 to 930^\circ\mathrm{C}) only adds carbon: the case reaches 0.8 to 1.0% C while the core stays at about 0.15 to 0.2% C. Cooled slowly, the case is pearlite (plus grain-boundary cementite), about 20 HRC, with no gain in wear resistance. Hardness appears only when the high-carbon austenite is quenched to martensite: case about 60 to 64 HRC, core low-carbon martensite or bainite for toughness. Because the case has the lower M_s, it transforms last and expands against the core, leaving useful compressive stress for fatigue. The long carburising time also coarsens the grain, which reheating refines.

Selecting the hardening temperature

The part is two steels with two critical temperatures:

  • Case (0.8 to 1.0% C): A_1 = 727^\circ\mathrm{C}; harden from A_1 + 30 to 50^\circ\mathrm{C}, about 760 to 780^\circ\mathrm{C}, for fine martensite, small spheroidal carbides and little retained austenite. Higher temperatures dissolve more carbon, lower M_s and leave soft retained austenite.
  • Core (0.15 to 0.2% C): A_3 \approx 840 to 860^\circ\mathrm{C}; harden from about 870 to 900^\circ\mathrm{C} for a fully transformed, strong core free of soft ferrite.

One temperature cannot suit both, so the choice follows the priority (case wear, core strength, distortion) and the cost.

Hardening and tempering schedules (A to D)

  • A, direct hardening: quench straight from carburising (often lowered to about 850^\circ\mathrm{C}). Cheapest, but coarse grain, more retained austenite and distortion; fine-grained steels only.
  • B, hardening after isothermal transformation: cool to and hold below \mathrm{Ac_1} (coarse austenite turns to ferrite + pearlite), reheat to just above the case critical temperature, about 780 to 800^\circ\mathrm{C}, quench. Refined, hard case; core only partly hardened.
  • C, single hardening: furnace-cool to room temperature, reheat just above the core \mathrm{Ac_3} (about 870^\circ\mathrm{C}), quench. Strong refined core, lower stresses and grinding-crack risk; case slightly coarse.
  • D, double hardening: reheat to about 880^\circ\mathrm{C} and quench (core refined), then to about 770^\circ\mathrm{C} and quench (case refined). Best properties, highest cost and distortion.

Cost rises from A to D. For pack-carburised plain-carbon bearing parts, direct quenching from the box is impractical and the steel is not fine grained, so the box is cooled and the parts reheated: once (C, or to about 780^\circ\mathrm{C} when the case matters most) or twice (D). Plain carbon needs a water or brine quench.

Temper every route at once at 150 to 180^\circ\mathrm{C}, 1 to 2 h: stresses relieved, case kept at about 60 HRC. Alloy carburised steels may need a cold treatment (-70 to -120^\circ\mathrm{C}) before tempering.

6b.html:
(i) Why the annealing schedules differ (10 marks)

  1. Graphite shape sets the aim. Grey-iron flakes act as notches, so the iron stays brittle whatever its matrix. Annealing only softens it for machining and removes carbide, and it costs about one grade (class 40 falls to class 30, book p 296). Nodular spheroids are not notches, so the matrix controls ductility. Annealing aims at a fully ferritic matrix to meet grades 60-45-12 and 60-40-18, so its cooling is tightly specified.
  2. Carbide. In grey iron free carbide is an accident (poor inoculation, carbide formers), so a graphitising anneal is not routine (book p 297). Nodular iron is Mg-treated, and Mg promotes carbide; thin or chill-cast parts often contain it, so graphitising and two-stage anneals are routine.
  3. Diffusion path. Grey-iron flakes form a network close to every part of the matrix, so carbon from pearlite reaches graphite quickly and a subcritical anneal ferritises it. In nodular iron carbon must travel to isolated nodules, so time depends on nodule count and section (1 h per inch), and ferrite needs slow cooling through the critical range.
  4. Composition. Nodular iron carries more Si, which raises the critical temperatures.

(ii) Austenitising temperature and quench hardness (7.5 marks)

Quenched hardness depends on the carbon in the martensite and on the martensite fraction. Graphite is a carbon reservoir, so the austenite carbon rises with austenitising temperature and falls with Si (book p 303):

\%C_0 = \frac{T_\gamma}{420} - 0.17\,\mathrm{Si} - 0.95

For 2.3% Si this gives about 0.60% C at 815^\circ\mathrm{C}, 0.73% at 870^\circ\mathrm{C} and 0.86% at 925^\circ\mathrm{C}.

  • Too low (800 to 845^\circ\mathrm{C}): low-carbon austenite, with some ferrite left near the critical range, gives soft martensite: about 20 to 45 HRC at 790 to 815^\circ\mathrm{C} (book Fig 6.8).
  • Optimum (about 870 to 900^\circ\mathrm{C}; 900^\circ\mathrm{C} for 2.5% Si): maximum hardness, about 55 HRC.
  • Too high: more carbon lowers M_s and M_f, retained austenite rises and hardness falls (about 47 HRC at 925^\circ\mathrm{C}), with more distortion.

Low-carbon martensite distorts less and is tougher after tempering (slide 14). Always temper.

7a.html:
Choice: resistance to wear and toughness.

Service conditions. A coal-mine drill bit cuts coal and the rock bands in it (shale, sandstone with quartz of about 1100 HV). It suffers abrasion by hard mineral particles and repeated impact, vibration and torsion from percussive or rotary drilling.

1. Resistance to wear (abrasion). Edge wear sets the bit's life. Wear resistance rises with hardness (book Fig 4.1) and, more strongly, with the amount of hard carbide: martensite (about 800 HV) is softer than quartz, while VC (about 3000 HV) and \mathrm{M_2C} (about 2000 HV) are harder (book Fig 4.12).

2. Toughness. Impact and vibration start cracks at the cutting point, and a brittle bit chips or snaps. Toughness also reduces wear: at equal hardness (65 HRC), tougher tool steels wear less (book Fig 4.5), because micro-chipping is itself a wear mechanism.

Why not the other two.

  • Hardness is a means to wear resistance, not a separate goal, and beyond about 60 HRC it costs toughness (more carbon and V make the steel brittle). A very hard but brittle bit fails by chipping.
  • Thermal-fatigue resistance matters for die-casting dies, forging dies and glass moulds, which are cycled against hot material (heat checking, slide 6). A drill bit is heated steadily by friction, not repeatedly heated and quenched.

Judgement in mechanical properties. The bit needs high fracture toughness and impact energy together with high abrasion resistance at a moderate hardness, about 55 to 60 HRC. This points to the shock-resisting group (S series: about 0.5% C with Si-Mo or Cr-W, 58 to 60 HRC; slide 10), hardened and tempered for toughness, with cemented-carbide inserts or hardfacing where the rock is very abrasive.

\mathrm{M_7C_3} (Cr-rich, hexagonal), not on the chart, is about 1600 to 1800 HV, close to \mathrm{M_6C}. Performance follows this order. Carbon-steel tools rely on martensite and \mathrm{Fe_3C}, about 4 to 5 times softer than alloy carbides, so they fail in heavy cutting.

Why the hardness differs

  1. Strength of the metal-carbon bond. Ti, Nb, V, Mo and W lie left of Fe in the transition series, with fewer d electrons, and bond carbon strongly with a large covalent share. Their carbides have high heats of formation, very high melting points (VC about 2800^\circ\mathrm{C}) and high hardness. Fe bonds carbon weakly: \mathrm{Fe_3C} is metastable and the softest. Cr lies between.
  2. Size ratio and crystal structure. When r_\mathrm{C}/r_\mathrm{M} < 0.59 (V, Mo, W, Ti, Nb: about 0.52 to 0.58) carbon fits the octahedral holes of a simple close-packed metal lattice: all of them in MC, half in \mathrm{M_2C}, giving a dense network of strong M-C bonds. Fe, Cr and Mn (ratio about 0.61 or more) form complex cells with fewer M-C bonds per atom (\mathrm{M_3C}, \mathrm{M_7C_3}, \mathrm{M_{23}C_6}). \mathrm{M_6C} is complex but rich in W or Mo, hence harder than the Cr carbides.
  3. Stability. Stable carbides (MC, \mathrm{M_6C}) resist dissolution and coarsening and stay hard at high temperature; unstable \mathrm{Fe_3C} coarsens and is replaced by Cr carbides during tempering (slides 19-21).

8a.html:
Softening and hardening tendency of HSS (10 marks)

As-quenched high-speed steel (M2, T1) is martensite with 20 to 30% retained austenite and undissolved carbides. On tempering, three effects overlap (slide 28):

  1. Softening of martensite: \varepsilon-carbide, then cementite, precipitate; carbon leaves the martensite and tetragonality is lost. Hardness falls steadily, and this dominates up to about 350 to 400^\circ\mathrm{C}.
  2. Transformation of retained austenite: from about 450 to 500^\circ\mathrm{C} carbides precipitate from the retained austenite, which loses C and alloy; its M_s rises and on cooling it becomes fresh, hard martensite.
  3. Precipitation of alloy carbides: above about 500^\circ\mathrm{C} W, Mo and V can diffuse and form ultrafine coherent \mathrm{M_2C} and MC on the dislocations of the martensite.

The total curve dips slightly, then rises to a secondary hardness peak at about 500 to 570^\circ\mathrm{C} that can exceed the as-quenched hardness (about 64.5 against 63.5 HRC in book Fig 4.31). Above about 600^\circ\mathrm{C} the carbides coarsen and hardness falls steeply. The peak gives red hardness; the fresh martensite needs tempering again, so HSS are tempered two or three times at 540 to 570^\circ\mathrm{C}.

Four classes of quenched tool steel (5 marks; slide 27)

  • Class 1, carbon and low-alloy tool steels: highest start, falls steadily as cementite precipitates and coarsens.
  • Class 2, medium- to high-alloy cold-work steels (A, D series): alloying retards carbide precipitation, so a plateau, then a drop.
  • Class 3, highly alloyed high-speed steels: strong secondary hardening; the peak can exceed the untempered hardness.
  • Class 4, medium- to high-alloy hot-work steels (H series): lower start because of lower carbon, then mild secondary hardening.

8b.html:
Cr (ferrite stabiliser) and C (austenite stabiliser) act oppositely on the \gamma field (slide 52):

  • Cr shrinks it into a closed loop whose lowest point (the eutectoid) rises and moves to lower carbon: 727^\circ\mathrm{C}/0.77% C at 0% Cr, about 795^\circ\mathrm{C}/0.5% C at 5% Cr, 845^\circ\mathrm{C}/0.4% C at 12% Cr.
  • Maximum carbon in austenite falls from about 2.1% to 1.35% (5% Cr) and 0.9% (12% Cr).
  • C widens the loop: carbon-free Fe-Cr loses austenite above about 12% Cr, yet with 0.3 to 0.6% C a small \gamma field survives at 15 to 19% Cr; hence martensitic stainless steels need carbon.

Maximum carbon solubility in austenite falls with Cr
Carbon extends the gamma field to higher Cr (gamma at 15 to 19% Cr only with about 0.3 to 0.6% C), the basis of martensitic stainless steels

8c.html:
What it is

Precipitation-hardenable (PH) stainless steels are low-carbon (at most about 0.1% C) Cr-Ni stainless steels, about 12 to 18% Cr and 4 to 9% Ni (about 25% Ni in A-286), that are hardened by an aging treatment. They are the fifth family, named after their heat treatment, not their microstructure. Al, Ti, Nb, Cu (with Mo, N) supply the precipitates. By the structure after solution annealing they are:

  • martensitic: 17-4 PH, 15-5 PH (Cu precipitates);
  • semi-austenitic: 17-7 PH, with 1.2% Al (NiAl, \mathrm{Ni_3Al});
  • austenitic: A-286 (\mathrm{Ni_3Ti}).

Why this class is needed

  • Austenitic and ferritic grades strengthen only by solid solution and work hardening: annealed YS 200 to 300 MPa; cold work is limited by shape and lost on welding.
  • Martensitic Fe-Cr-C grades get strength from carbon: high C lowers ductility and toughness, ties Cr up in carbides (poorest corrosion resistance) and needs a distortion-prone quench.
  • PH steels fill this gap: YS up to about 1700 MPa with toughness and corrosion resistance, machined soft and then aged with little distortion (springs, knives, aerospace parts).

How hardening occurs

  1. Solution treatment at 980 to 1065^\circ\mathrm{C} (Condition A): the alloy is single-phase and all precipitate formers dissolve.
  2. Cooling fast enough to keep a supersaturated solid solution; martensitic grades become low-C lath martensite without retained austenite.
  3. Aging at 450 to 620^\circ\mathrm{C}: the solution decomposes into fine coherent clusters. Their size mismatch strains the lattice and pins dislocations; larger semi-coherent or incoherent particles are passed only by bowing between them.
  4. Strength rises to a peak, then falls with overaging (coarsening). Example 17-4 PH: tensile strength about 1310 MPa after 1 h at 480^\circ\mathrm{C}, 930 MPa after 4 h at 620^\circ\mathrm{C}.

8c.watch:
• "Why do we need" is a comparison: name both alternatives (solid solution plus cold work, and carbon martensite) and say what each lacks.
  • Semi-austenitic grades need an extra conditioning step (about 760^\circ\mathrm{C}, which precipitates \mathrm{Cr_{23}C_6} and raises M_s, then cooling below about 15^\circ\mathrm{C}) before aging; mentioning it shows the difference between the types.
  • Do not confuse this with tempering of carbon martensite: the strength comes from intermetallic or Cu precipitates, not from carbon.
